name: Onion juice

lead: Onion juice is pressed from onion bulbs and applied to the scalp as a natural way to regrow hair and thicken thinning areas. It circulates in social-media hair advice alongside rosemary oil and rice water.

The idea is that it stimulates follicles, with antioxidant effects and improved circulation proposed as general explanations. A small 2002 controlled trial in patchy alopecia areata reported more regrowth with onion juice than with tap water, and reviews describe the wider literature as small samples, mostly combination products.

paras: People apply the juice to the scalp, often as a mask or in a leave-in, a few times a week and leave it on before washing. Results are judged over months, and it is often combined with other natural or conventional hair treatments.
The sources report no specific safety data for scalp use. It is an unregulated food-derived preparation, and strong smell and skin irritation are common complaints. Reviews call for further study.

angle.text: Onion juice is applied to the scalp in the hope of stimulating follicles for regrowth and denser hair, often alongside rosemary oil. One small 2002 trial in alopecia areata reported more regrowth than water; trials in pattern baldness have not been done.

lead: Onion juice is the liquid pressed from the bulb of the common onion (Allium cepa), applied to the scalp as a folk remedy for hair loss and to encourage hair growth. It is discussed in reviews of social-media hair-loss advice alongside rosemary oil, rice water and garlic gel.[1][2]

The best-known clinical evidence is a small 2002 controlled trial in patchy alopecia areata, in which participants applying crude onion juice twice daily for two months were reported to show more regrowth than those applying tap water.[3] Narrative reviews describe the wider literature as limited by small samples, lack of comparison with standard treatments, and conflicts of interest, and note that onion juice has mostly been studied in combination products.[4][2] A 2025 review of online alopecia misinformation lists onion juice among the unproven natural remedies promoted online.[5]

paras: In hair-care communities onion juice is applied to the scalp with the aim of promoting regrowth, thickening or reducing shedding. Reviews of herbal and topical hair products identify it as one of several popular plant-derived actives, together with rosemary oil, saw palmetto and pumpkin seed oil.[4][2]

A 2002 controlled trial in patchy alopecia areata compared crude onion juice (23 patients) with tap water (15 patients) applied twice daily for two months. The authors reported regrowth of coarse terminal hair beginning at about two weeks, in 73.9% of the onion juice group at four weeks and 86.9% at six weeks, versus 13% of the water group at eight weeks.[3] It was a small, single-report study, and reviews note that the broader literature on topical botanicals tends to have small samples, nonuniform groups, and undisclosed alopecia types.[4]

A 2025 review of herbal remedies for hair loss includes onion juice among agents that studies suggest may promote hair growth, while calling for more rigorous evidence.[2] A review of TikTok hair-loss remedies examined the evidence behind onion juice, rosemary oil, rice water and garlic gel.[1] Other human trials of onion juice found in searches concern drinking it (for example, effects on bone markers or cholesterol) and do not address hair.[6][7]
Beyond hair, onion juice has been studied in laboratory and animal work, for example on platelet aggregation in dogs and on experimental cataract in rats, none of which bears on hair growth.[8][9]

Onion juice features in reviews of social-media-driven hair-loss advice. Authors of one review describe sponsored marketing and social platforms as drivers of interest in hair serums and oils,[4] and a qualitative review of online alopecia information lists onion juice among natural remedies it characterises as lacking support.[5]

lore.intro: Onion juice appears in social-media hair-loss advice as a natural alternative to conventional treatments.[1][5]
